title: Margin vs Markup: Calculator, Formula & Examples
description: Calculate margin and markup, compare discounts and find the selling price for your target. Use worked examples and clear formulas on one cost basis.
metaDescription: Calculate margin and markup, compare discounts and find the selling price for your target. Use worked examples and clear formulas on one cost basis.
alt: Retail owner comparing supplier cost, markup, and selling price at a counter
imageCaption: Retail owner comparing supplier cost, markup, and selling price at a counter
opening: Learn margin vs markup with clear formulas, realistic examples, and pricing steps so you can set prices accurately and avoid costly mistakes.
features: Assumptions and cost behavior made visible
html:
If you confuse margin vs markup, you can price a profitable-looking sale too low or misread how much money your business actually keeps. Markup is the percentage you add to your cost; margin is the percentage of your selling price that remains after cost, so the two percentages are not interchangeable.

Quick answer: Markup starts with cost and tells you how much you add to reach a price. Margin starts with the selling price and tells you how much of that price is gross profit. A 50% markup does not create a 50% margin: $100 of cost becomes a $150 price, leaving $50, or 33.3% margin.

The margin and markup formulas

The simplest way to remember the difference is to ask what number sits underneath the percentage.

Markup uses cost as its base:

> Markup = (Selling price − Cost) ÷ Cost × 100

If an item costs you $40 and you sell it for $60, your gross profit is $20. Your markup is $20 ÷ $40, or 50%.

Margin uses selling price as its base:

> Margin = (Selling price − Cost) ÷ Selling price × 100

With the same $40 cost and $60 price, your margin is $20 ÷ $60, or 33.3%.

Both calculations use the same gross profit dollars. They answer different questions. Markup asks, “How much did I add to my cost?” Margin asks, “What share of my revenue is left after the direct cost?”

That distinction matters when you set prices, compare products, plan discounts, or estimate the money available for overhead. A business owner who says “I need a 40% margin” cannot simply add 40% to cost. To set a target margin, you must work backward from the selling price.

The conversion formulas are useful:

  • Margin from markup: Markup ÷ (1 + Markup)
  • Markup from margin: Margin ÷ (1 − Margin)

Use decimals in those formulas. A 40% markup is 0.40 ÷ 1.40, or 28.6% margin. A 40% margin requires 0.40 ÷ 0.60, or 66.7% markup.

Neither measure includes every business expense automatically. Product cost, direct labor, payment processing, shipping, packaging, or other variable costs may need to be included depending on what decision you are making. Be clear about whether you are calculating a product’s gross margin or the business’s final profit.

What changes the answer

The right percentage depends on your purpose and cost definition. A retailer may calculate markup to build a shelf price from wholesale cost. A service business may focus on margin after direct labor and materials. A restaurant may include ingredients and direct preparation costs when reviewing menu economics.

Start by defining “cost.” For a physical product, that might include purchase cost, inbound freight, packaging, and per-unit handling. For a cleaning job, direct labor and supplies may belong in the job cost. For a menu item, ingredients and packaging can be relevant. Do not switch between a narrow product cost and a broader delivered cost while comparing percentages.

Your sales channel also changes the price you need. A direct sale, marketplace sale, wholesale order, and sale through a representative may each have different fees or commissions. If a channel takes a percentage of revenue, calculate the fee before deciding that a target margin is met. A price that works in your store may not work after a marketplace fee.

Discounts change the result too. If your list price is $100 and you offer 20% off, your customer pays $80. A cost of $50 creates $30 gross profit. That is a 60% markup on cost, but only a 37.5% margin on the discounted selling price. The discount did not merely reduce revenue; it reduced the margin rate.

Taxes deserve care. Sales tax collected for an authority is generally not your sales revenue, while income tax is considered later in the profit picture. Keep those concepts separate in your worksheet.

Use the measure your audience understands. If a supplier asks for a markup, respond with markup. If you are setting a gross-margin target, calculate margin. When in doubt, show dollars as well as percentage: cost, price, gross profit, margin, and markup together remove ambiguity.

Worked examples: converting margin and markup

Scenario 1: A product sale

You buy a product for $24 and sell it for $36.

  • Gross profit: $36 − $24 = $12
  • Markup: $12 ÷ $24 = 50%
  • Margin: $12 ÷ $36 = 33.3%

If you want a 50% margin, do not price it at $36. Use the target-margin formula:

> Price = Cost ÷ (1 − Target margin)

So the required price is $24 ÷ (1 − 0.50) = $48. At $48, gross profit is $24, which is 50% of the selling price. The markup is 100%.

Scenario 2: A house-cleaning job

Suppose a two-hour cleaning job has $44 of direct labor and $6 of supplies, for a direct cost of $50. You quote $80.

  • Gross profit: $80 − $50 = $30
  • Markup: $30 ÷ $50 = 60%
  • Margin: $30 ÷ $80 = 37.5%

The $30 is not necessarily take-home profit. It may need to cover scheduling time, insurance, software, travel that was not included in the job cost, advertising, rent, and other operating expenses. For more context on building a service price, see ways to lower your break-even point.

If your goal is a 45% margin on the defined $50 direct cost, the quote would be $50 ÷ 0.55 = $90.91. Gross profit would be $40.91, and $40.91 ÷ $90.91 is 45%.

Scenario 3: A restaurant menu item

A menu item has ingredient and direct packaging costs of $8. You price it at $20.

  • Gross profit: $20 − $8 = $12
  • Markup: $12 ÷ $8 = 150%
  • Margin: $12 ÷ $20 = 60%

That 60% margin is based only on the costs you included. It does not prove the item is profitable after payroll, rent, utilities, delivery fees, waste, and other expenses. Use the result to compare menu items consistently, then review the broader business numbers. This calculate your break-even point explains the pricing logic in a menu setting.

A margin-versus-markup worksheet you can check

Put your defined unit cost in A2 and actual selling price in B2. These formulas work in Excel or Google Sheets; they are instructions for your own sheet, not a downloadable template. Format ratio cells as percentages without also multiplying by 100.

One sale, two denominators
OutputFormulaCost $70; price $100
Profit on the stated cost basis=B2-A2$30
Markup on cost=(B2-A2)/A242.86%
Margin on sales=(B2-A2)/B230%

For a target margin entered as 30% in C2, price is =A2/(1-C2). With a separate 3% fee in D2, it becomes =A2/(1-C2-D2), provided the cost in A2 excludes that fee and the denominator is positive. $70 ÷ 0.67 requires $104.48 when rounded upward to cents. This is margin after the defined costs, not automatically accounting gross or net margin.

Zero cost makes percentage markup undefined; zero revenue makes margin undefined. A zero-cost item sold for a positive price can have 100% margin on that narrow cost basis but still incur selling costs. Do not replace undefined results with a reassuring 0%. For a discounted offer, substitute the collected price and use discount volume recovery to check the extra sales needed.

How to run your own numbers

Make a small table for each product, job, or service. Put the unit cost in one column, the actual selling price in another, and calculate gross profit as price minus cost. Then calculate both percentages so you can see whether someone has used the wrong term.

For a current sale, use:

  • Gross profit = Price − Cost
  • Markup = Gross profit ÷ Cost
  • Margin = Gross profit ÷ Price

For a target markup, use:

> Price = Cost × (1 + Markup)

A $70 cost with a 30% markup produces a $91 price: $70 × 1.30. Gross profit is $21, so margin is $21 ÷ $91, or about 23.1%.

For a target margin, use:

> Price = Cost ÷ (1 − Margin)

A $70 cost with a 30% margin requires $100: $70 ÷ 0.70. Gross profit is $30, exactly 30% of $100.

Enter the numbers in the MyBreakeven calculator to test price, cost, and break-even assumptions together. Round the customer-facing price only after doing the calculation. Then recalculate from the rounded price, because rounding can change the actual margin.

Run a second version that includes variable fees. For example, if a sale has a $5 cost and a 10% marketplace fee, a target margin cannot be checked by subtracting only $5. Use a consistent formula for the fee and price. If the fee is a percentage of price, solve for the price rather than guessing.

Finally, test a range of prices. Compare the expected gross profit dollars, not just the percentage. A lower-margin item may produce more dollars if it sells in much greater volume, while a high-margin item may be slow or expensive to sell. Pricing is a decision about both economics and demand; the calculation gives you a clear floor, not a guaranteed sales forecast.

Common mistakes

Calling markup margin. This is the classic error. Always identify whether the denominator is cost or selling price.

Adding a target margin to cost. Adding 40% to cost creates a 28.6% margin, not a 40% margin. Use cost divided by one minus the target margin.

Ignoring discounts. Evaluate the price customers actually pay, not just the list price. If discounts are common, build them into your pricing decision.

Leaving out direct costs. Materials, direct labor, packaging, freight, commissions, and transaction fees can materially change the result. Define your cost consistently.

Treating gross margin as net profit. Gross profit still has to support overhead and other expenses. A strong product margin does not guarantee a profitable company.

Rounding too early. Keep full precision through the calculation, then round the final price and verify the result.

Comparing unlike calculations. One product’s margin may include shipping and fees while another’s includes only purchase cost. Use the same cost rules before drawing conclusions. For more practical pricing guidance, explore the small business guide library.

Using a percentage without dollars. A percentage can sound impressive while the gross profit dollars are too small to support your operation. Show both.

Closing takeaways

  1. Markup is based on cost; margin is based on selling price.
  2. A target margin requires division by one minus the margin, not a simple addition to cost.
  3. Include the direct costs and channel fees that belong to the decision.
  4. Check the actual discounted price and report dollars alongside percentages.
  5. Use margin and markup together when you want pricing decisions that are easy to explain and hard to misread.

Preserve a target margin after a planned discount

If cost is $70 and the target margin is 30%, the required collected selling price is $100. To offer 20% off while retaining that price, the list price is $100 ÷ 0.80 = $125. Marking a $100 item down by 20% instead collects $80, leaving $10 and a 12.5% margin on the same $70 cost.

The markup versus margin calculator rounds a target selling-price floor upward to cents, then rounds the discount-adjusted list-price floor upward. Recheck the collected price against the defined cost. At a 100% discount, no finite list price can collect a positive target selling price. These price floors do not predict demand or extra sales.

For the basic denominator distinction, see AccountingCoach’s margin and markup explanation. The discount-adjusted list-price example above is an original application of the stated formulas.

faq.q: Is a 50% markup the same as a 50% margin?
faq.a: No. A 50% markup means a $100 cost becomes a $150 price, creating $50 gross profit. The margin is $50 ÷ $150, or 33.3%. A 50% margin on a $100 cost requires a $200 price, which is a 100% markup.

faq.q: Which is better for pricing: margin or markup?
faq.a: Use the measure that matches the decision. Markup is convenient when you start with cost and add an amount. Margin is useful when you need a defined share of revenue left after direct cost. Many businesses track both to avoid confusion.

faq.q: How do I convert markup to margin?
faq.a: Divide the markup by one plus the markup. For a 25% markup, calculate 0.25 ÷ 1.25 = 20% margin. The reverse is margin divided by one minus margin.

faq.q: Can margin be higher than 100%?
faq.a: For a standard sale with positive cost, gross margin cannot exceed 100% because gross profit is part of the selling price. Markup can exceed 100% when the selling price is more than twice the cost.

faq.q: Should labor be included in cost?
faq.a: Include direct labor when you are evaluating the economics of a job or service. Whether to include owner time, overhead, or administrative labor depends on the question. State your cost definition and use it consistently.

faq.q: Why does my margin fall after a discount?
faq.a: A discount lowers the selling price while the direct cost may stay the same. Since margin divides gross profit by the lower selling price, both the gross-profit dollars and margin percentage usually decline.

faq.q: Do I need both numbers in my reports?
faq.a: Keeping both can help, especially when suppliers, sales staff, and managers use different terminology. At minimum, show cost, selling price, gross profit dollars, and the percentage label so the calculation is transparent.

title: Is a Cleaning Business Profitable? Check the Visits and Hours
description: Test cleaning business profit from visit contribution, monthly bills and owner pay. Compare labor overruns, recurring work, re-cleans and staff capacity.

opening: A cleaning business can be profitable when its completed visits cover delivery costs, monthly bills and the owner’s income. In the example below, a $160 visit contributes $63.20, but the 95 visits needed for the income goal exceed the two-person team's assumed capacity.
features: Gross, contribution, and net margin separated
Owner take-home kept distinct from accounting profit
Capacity and utilization checked against revenue goals
html:
A cleaning business can be profitable when its completed visits cover delivery costs, monthly bills and the owner’s income. In the example below, a $160 visit contributes $63.20, but the 95 visits needed for the income goal exceed the two-person team's assumed capacity.

That is why a full diary deserves a closer look. Check what each visit leaves and how many worker-hours it uses, then see whether the monthly target can fit. The USD figures here are illustrative; use your own completed visits, paid labor and route records.

Is a cleaning business profitable? Start with profit per visit

A cleaning business can be profitable when the contribution from completed cleaning visits covers recurring overhead, owner compensation included in the plan, and any other committed expenses. Revenue and a busy calendar alone are not proof of profit. Subtract direct labor, supplies, travel and other visit-level costs from the amount collected, then compare the remainder with monthly commitments and realistic staff capacity.

In the fictional example further below, a $160 completed visit leaves $63.20 before monthly commitments. The income-goal scenario needs 95 completed visits, but that exceeds the stated two-person team capacity. This is a capacity-limited example, not an industry-wide profit margin or earnings promise. Calculate the cleaning visits and revenue needed with your own costs, then review the worked assumptions below.

Quick answer

Calculate contribution for one complete visit, including paid worker time, supplies, travel-related costs, acquisition and payment fees. Divide the monthly fixed-cost, owner-pay and profit goal by that contribution and round up to whole visits. Compare the required visits with worker-hour capacity and realistic paid demand. A plan is stronger when the same assumptions fit all three checks.

Start with the visits you finish and get paid for

Separate recurring maintenance cleans, first visits and move-out jobs. Their preparation and task lists can differ enough to make one average misleading. For each type, record the agreed scope, price, actual worker-hours and any return visit needed to complete the work.

Count the crew's time, not only the customer's appointment length. Two cleaners working 1.5 hours use three worker-hours. If paid travel and setup sit outside that time, add them to both the cost and duration used in the plan.

Use completed paid visits as the sales unit. Keep inquiries, bookings and cancellations in separate columns. A booking that drops out may still cost acquisition money or leave a gap in the route, but it does not produce the full completed-visit revenue in this example.

When the customer changes the requested work, update the visit record and quote before assuming the same margin. Another room or a task outside the scope can increase supplies and time even if the diary still shows one appointment.

For owner income, settle the pay method once. This example includes paid staff labor per visit and a separate owner-pay goal. A solo cleaner may instead put their income in owner pay; including the same wage again in direct labor would overstate the cost.

With those definitions in place, you can compare the quote with the visit you actually delivered. A short job note about access, travel or added tasks is enough to explain many of the differences without turning the review into a long report.

Calculate the contribution from one cleaning visit

Per-visit input Example input
Selling price $160
Materials and cleaning supplies $8
Paid direct labor: 3 worker-hours × $22 $66
Other variable cost, including allocated travel expense $10
Acquisition cost per completed visit $8
Payment fee at 3% $4.80
Contribution $63.20

Before the percentage fee, direct costs total $92. Contribution is $160 − $92 − $4.80 = $63.20 per completed visit. The contribution margin is $63.20 ÷ $160 = 39.5%. This does not mean the owner keeps 39.5% as final profit.

The supply input should represent the portion used on one visit, not an entire restocking purchase. Acquisition cost should reflect the completed paid visits used in your planning period. A recurring customer's initial acquisition cost can be allocated across an explicitly chosen number of visits, while a new one-time customer may carry a different cost.

The $10 other-cost input is an assumed job allocation. If it includes vehicle expenses that are already fully charged in monthly fixed costs, remove the overlap. Re-clean costs are set to zero in the base visit and tested separately below. That makes the starting calculation transparent rather than quietly assuming no job will ever need additional work.

Show the monthly profit after owner pay

Assume monthly fixed costs $2,500, owner pay $3,000 and target profit $500. The goal is $6,000. At $63.20 contribution, required volume is $6,000 ÷ $63.20 = 94.94, rounded up to 95 completed visits.

At exactly 95 visits, revenue is $15,200 and contribution is $6,004. After fixed costs and owner pay, planning profit is $504. The planning profit margin is $504 ÷ $15,200 = 3.32%. This shows the difference between a 39.5% contribution margin and the much smaller amount remaining after the monthly requirements.

At 100 visits, contribution is $6,320 and planning profit after those same requirements is $820, or 5.13% of $16,000 revenue. At 80 visits, contribution is $5,056 and the business is $444 short of covering fixed costs plus the $3,000 owner-pay goal. The individual visit still has positive contribution in all three cases; monthly volume changes the overall result.

Keep cash timing separate when commercial customers pay after invoicing. Completed work can be profitable on the job worksheet while payroll and supply payments arrive before customer cash. Record receipts and payment dates instead of assuming every invoiced dollar is available immediately.

Compare price, labor and re-clean scenarios

Scenario Price Direct cost before fee Contribution Visits for $6,000 goal
Base three-hour visit $160 $92 $63.20 95
Same visit at $175 $175 $92 $77.75 78
Labor rises to four worker-hours $160 $114 $41.20 146
Base visit plus $5 expected re-clean cost $160 $97 $58.20 104

The price increase leaves $14.55 more contribution per visit after the fee adjustment. It is a controlled offer scenario, not a prediction of customer acceptance. If the higher price includes extra work, include that work's costs and hours before claiming the same benefit.

The labor-overrun case adds one worker-hour at $22 and removes delivery capacity. Its required volume rises to 146 visits. The $5 re-clean allowance instead represents an expected cost allocated across completed visits. If it comes from actual records, use the frequency and average additional cost consistently. If it is an untested assumption, label it and compare a higher-cost case.

Re-cleans can consume schedule time as well as cash. The table isolates the contribution effect; the capacity scenario must include the expected extra worker-hours when testing the full plan. A cost allowance without time can hide the disruption caused by returning to a property.

Compare required visits with staff capacity

Two workers with 35 weekly hours each at 70% utilization provide 2 × 35 × 52 ÷ 12 × 70% = 212.33 monthly delivery worker-hours. At three worker-hours per visit, whole-visit capacity is 70. The base requirement of 95 visits therefore exceeds capacity even though every visit contributes positively.

At four worker-hours, capacity falls to 53 while required volume rises to 146. The labor overrun hurts both sides of the plan. Changing only the hourly capacity figure or only the labor cost misses part of the problem.

At the $175 price, 78 visits are still more than the same 70-visit capacity. If the scope can be delivered in 2.5 worker-hours without compromising the agreed work, capacity would be 84. That is a separate operational scenario that requires evidence from completed jobs, not an instruction to rush the service.

Three workers at 35 weekly hours and 70% utilization would provide 318.5 hours and 106 whole three-hour visits. The hour requirement could then fit, but additional fixed costs, hiring constraints and paid demand might change the goal. Recalculate the full plan when adding people rather than treating capacity as free.

Use recurring work without overstating the benefit

A repeat customer may reduce acquisition and scheduling effort, but recurring pricing can also be lower. Compare both sides. Suppose repeat visits carry $3 in allocated acquisition rather than $8 while the price remains $160. Contribution improves to $68.20. If the recurring price falls to $150, contribution becomes $58.50 with that same $3 acquisition cost.

The recurring label alone therefore does not establish a better margin. Track actual visit duration, cancellations, route grouping and retained paid customers. When a customer leaves, replacement acquisition can increase again. Keep first visits and ongoing visits separate before building a weighted average.

A route with several nearby properties can reduce travel, but only if the completed schedule supports the allocation. If one customer cancels, the remaining trip may need more time or cost per visit. Record the actual route outcome rather than assuming every recurring slot produces the same efficiency.

Compare cleaning payroll ratios without inventing a benchmark

An average cleaning-company revenue figure needs a dated sample, business size, service mix and geography. This guide does not establish such an average. Use the completed-visit revenue and owner-pay reconciliation already worked above rather than interpreting revenue as take-home income.

For an isolated payroll-ratio sensitivity, fictional loaded field payroll of $8,000 divided by $20,000 matching net sales is 40%. The same payroll against $16,000 sales is 50%. Neither 40% nor 50% here is a survey benchmark. A query containing 40–60 does not make that range a verified industry rule.

Match payroll and sales periods, state whether employer costs and owner cleaning time are included, and separate residential recurring work from commercial contracts before comparing businesses. Keep the existing visit-level example for the complete profit and capacity calculation.

Cost a commercial cleaning contract · Build a cleaning expense budget

Track cleaning-company profit from completed work

A quote calculator tests a plan; a monthly review needs records of the work actually delivered. Keep one row per completed visit with its job ID, service type, net charge after discounts or refunds, total paid worker-hours, labor cost, supplies used, travel allocation, acquisition cost and payment fee. Link any re-clean to the original job. Add invoice and collection dates in separate fields so unpaid sales do not quietly become bank cash.

Close the same reporting period for sales, staff costs and overhead. Separate an estimate from an actual amount, and flag a missing supplier or payroll record rather than filling the gap with zero. A supply purchase can cover several months: the per-visit schedule needs the portion used, while the cash review needs the payment. Retain the source record behind each allocation.

Independent fictional month: 70 completed visits, USD
Management-report lineReconciliationAmount
Net visit revenue70 × $160$11,200
Paid staff labor70 × 3.4 worker-hours × $22($5,236)
Supplies used70 × $8($560)
Other variable costs70 × $10($700)
Acquisition allocation70 × $8($560)
Payment fees$11,200 × 3%($336)
Contribution$11,200 − $7,392$3,808
Specified fixed operating costsSame $2,500 scope as the base plan($2,500)
Operating surplus before owner compensation and omitted items$3,808 − $2,500$1,308
Separate owner-income funding target$1,308 − $3,000($1,692) shortfall

The labor record is the important change: each visit uses 3.4 worker-hours instead of the base plan’s three. At 70 visits, the extra 28 worker-hours cost $616. At the original three-hour assumption, those same visits would contribute $4,424; subtracting the $616 labor overrun reconciles to $3,808. The plan for 95 visits would leave $504 after its $3,000 owner-income target. The revised month is $2,196 below that result: $1,580 from 25 fewer visits at $63.20 contribution, plus $616 extra labor. This bridge isolates volume and labor under the stated unchanged assumptions; it does not prove why jobs took longer.

Check capacity as well as the ledger. Seventy visits at 3.4 worker-hours require 238 worker-hours, exceeding the base team’s 212.33 delivery hours by 25.67. If the records genuinely show this month’s 70 visits, document overtime, extra staffing or a different available-hours schedule and include the related costs. Do not call the original two-person schedule feasible merely because the profit table reconciles.

The $3,000 owner-income target is shown after operating surplus as a planning requirement. It is not automatically a payroll expense. In a sole-proprietor example, personal drawings belong in a separate owner/cash record; IRS Publication 334, Employees’ Pay explains the US tax distinction between employee pay and a sole proprietor’s own withdrawals. Other entity and payroll arrangements need their own treatment. This simplified schedule excludes taxes, financing, depreciation and any unlisted owner labor or expenses, so $1,308 is not certified net income.

Finish the review with an action tied to the record: inspect scope changes on jobs with excess hours, correct duplicate travel allocations, investigate re-cleans, and compare recurring and one-time services separately. Use the estimate-versus-actual job worksheet for individual visits and the monthly cleaning budget for the period. The net cash flow calculator checks actual receipts and payments; a profitable month does not guarantee that every invoice was collected.

Enter the base visit in the calculator

Open the cleaning business break-even calculator. Enter price $160, material cost $8, labor cost $66, other variable cost $10, acquisition cost $8 and payment fee 3%. Use fixed costs $2,500, owner pay $3,000 and target profit $500.

Set two workers, 35 weekly hours per worker, three total worker-hours per visit and 70% utilization. The example should show $63.20 contribution, 95 required visits and 70 whole-visit capacity. Change both labor cost and hours per visit for an overrun. Save distinct one-time and recurring scenarios when their inputs differ.

What a full cleaning diary can hide

  • Equating bookings with completed paid visits. Cancellations and unpaid work change revenue and acquisition cost.
  • Ignoring crew-hours. Two workers multiply labor even when the customer sees a short appointment.
  • Calling contribution take-home profit. Fixed costs and owner income still need coverage.
  • Reducing time without evidence. Capacity assumptions must preserve the agreed service scope.
  • Assuming recurring work is automatically better. Compare price, acquisition, route time and retention together.

Track cleaning-company profit from completed visits, not bookings alone

A profit-tracking record needs a stable job ID, quoted scope, completed status, actual paid worker-hours, materials, travel, fees, invoice credits and collection status. Keep a cancellation separate from a completed visit and identify an unpaid completed invoice rather than silently removing it from accrual sales. Reconcile paid cash in a separate collections column.

Independent fictional ten-booking review, USD
RecordCalculationAmount
Scheduled work10 bookings at 1801,800 potential sales
Completed and collected work9 visits at 180; one uncharged cancellation1,620 sales and collections
Paid labor including travel27 on-site worker-hours + 3 travel hours, at loaded 25750
Other visit-driven costs9 × 15135
Included monthly overheadSeparate fixed amount300
Operating result after stated labor and costs1,620 − 750 − 135 − 300435

The 26.85% operating margin is a result of these invented inputs, not an average cleaning-company margin. The loaded labor amount already pays for the work, including owner delivery labor if modeled that way. Do not subtract that same work again as a second owner wage. Interest, tax and unentered costs must be reconciled before calling a result net profit or take-home cash.

Record re-cleans and unpaid travel as work even if they do not produce another invoice. Compare completed visits, actual labor and contribution with the monthly expense budget. An increase in bookings or annual revenue alone does not prove that a cleaning business is more profitable.

FAQs

Can every visit make money while the business misses its income goal?

Yes, positive contribution from a visit is only part of the test. The month also needs enough completed work to cover fixed bills and the chosen owner income, within the available worker-hours.

How many completed visits does this example need?

The $6,000 combined goal needs 95 visits at $63.20 contribution each. The assumed two-worker schedule supports 70 whole visits, so the base plan needs a change in price, cost, scope or available delivery hours.

What happens when a three-hour visit takes four worker-hours?

At the example’s $22 hourly labor cost, contribution falls from $63.20 to $41.20. The longer duration also reduces whole-visit capacity from 70 to 53 under the same team schedule.

How should I record a re-clean?

Link its additional time and costs to the original completed visit. Use the recorded frequency and cost to create an allowance, and include the expected hours when checking capacity.

Should I automatically discount recurring visits?

Compare the reduction in acquisition, travel or service time with the contribution lost to the discount. The example’s $150 recurring visit leaves less contribution than the $160 base visit despite its lower acquisition allowance.

What should I review before adding another cleaner?

Recalculate paid labor, any added fixed costs and the jobs the larger team can deliver. Then check whether enough paid work is available to use those hours; the extra capacity alone does not cover its costs.

Takeaways

  • Use completed paid visits, with a separate record of cancellations.
  • Count all workers' delivery and relevant travel time.
  • Include re-clean costs and the hours needed to return.
  • Compare the monthly income target with paid demand and deliverable visits.

Continue with the cleaning monthly expenses guide, recurring versus one-time cleaning guide and cleaning client churn guide. Browse the business guides for more examples.

answerHtml:
Compare cleaning payroll ratios without inventing a benchmark

A cleaning business is profitable when revenue covers delivery costs and the included operating commitments. Revenue alone does not show what the owner keeps. Calculate payroll percentage from a defined payroll numerator and the same period’s net sales.

name: Landscaping
title: Landscaping Profit Margin: Follow the Money Behind Each Job
description: Calculate landscaping profit margin with direct costs, fees, overhead and owner pay. Compare price changes, monthly job goals and delivery capacity.
metaDescription: Calculate landscaping profit margin with direct costs, fees, overhead and owner pay. Compare price changes, monthly job goals and delivery capacity.
alt: Landscaping business owner reviewing profit margin and operating costs
imageCaption: Landscaping business owner reviewing profit margin and operating costs
opening: The example crew invoices $18,000 for 40 jobs and has $3,260 left after the listed job costs, fees, overhead and owner pay. Its planning profit margin is 18.11%, while the contribution margin before those monthly requirements is 57%.
features: Gross, contribution, and net margin separated
Owner take-home kept distinct from accounting profit
Capacity and utilization checked against revenue goals
html:
The example crew invoices $18,000 for 40 jobs and has $3,260 left after the listed job costs, fees, overhead and owner pay. Its planning profit margin is 18.11%, while the contribution margin before those monthly requirements is 57%.

Keep those two percentages separate when reviewing the business. The first tells you what the month leaves after the chosen pay treatment; the second tells you what the jobs contribute toward it. This guide uses illustrative USD figures and follows the hours behind the revenue, including price cuts and higher job costs.

Quick answer

State whether you mean job contribution, operating profit or profit after a chosen owner-pay goal. Use consistent revenue and cost definitions, include the relevant crew and equipment costs, then divide the resulting profit by revenue. Check the same plan against worker-hours and actual completed jobs. A positive margin percentage alone does not show whether the monthly income goal is achievable.

Put the cost list beside the margin percentage

Start the review with completed jobs and the revenue they brought in. Then subtract the costs that follow those jobs: materials, paid crew labor, other job expenses, acquisition and payment fees. The amount left is contribution toward the month's bills and income goals.

For this guide, monthly planning profit is total contribution minus fixed costs and the separately stated owner-pay goal. Write that definition beside the result. It gives you a repeatable comparison from month to month even when another report uses a different profit measure.

Choose how to handle the owner’s field time. If the direct labor line already pays for those hours, leave the identical pay out of the owner-pay goal. A solo operator can instead use owner pay for that income and exclude the same personal wage from direct job labor. Changing the method between months can make profit appear to move when only the classification changed.

Keep cash purchases and accounting items in their appropriate records. Buying a mower, paying loan principal and using equipment during a job are different events. This worksheet focuses on operating contribution and the chosen monthly pay goal; a separate cash plan should show when larger payments leave the bank.

Once the definition is settled, compare services. You can see which job types bring in the contribution and which absorb the hours. That is more useful than an overall percentage with no record of the work behind it.

Build the example monthly result

The example completes 40 jobs at $450 each. Each job has the following costs before percentage payment fees:

Per-job input Example amount
Materials $30
Paid direct crew labor $100
Other variable costs, including allocated equipment and travel $35
Acquisition cost per completed job $15
Total direct job cost before fee $180
Payment fee at 3% of $450 $13.50
Job contribution $256.50

At 40 completed jobs, revenue is $18,000 and direct costs before fees are $7,200. Payment fees total $540. Contribution is $18,000 − $7,200 − $540 = $10,260, or 57% of revenue.

Monthly fixed costs are $4,000 and the remaining owner-pay goal is $3,000. Profit after these bills and owner pay is $10,260 − $4,000 − $3,000 = $3,260. The planning profit margin is $3,260 ÷ $18,000 = 18.11%.

If you stop at contribution and call the 57% figure net profit, you hide $7,000 of monthly requirements. If you compare the 18.11% figure with another business that handles owner compensation differently, the comparison can also mislead. Keep the costs and compensation treatment next to the percentage.

Include equipment and route costs once

Equipment use can enter the model as a job-level allocation, a monthly fixed cost, or a combination covering different items. State what each line includes. For instance, fuel and job-specific wear may sit in other variable costs while recurring insurance and storage remain fixed. Do not include the same replacement allowance in both lines.

Use actual worker-hours for crew labor. Two workers on a two-hour site job use four worker-hours, before any additional paid route time. A $100 labor cost for four hours implies a $25 hourly cost. If paid preparation or travel adds time, increase the labor cost and capacity duration accordingly.

Acquisition spending needs a relevant denominator. Suppose a campaign costs $300 and generates 20 inquiries but only ten paid jobs. The cost per completed job is $30, not $15. Estimating from inquiry count alone can overstate contribution when conversion is weaker than expected.

Keep maintenance routes and installation jobs separate if their economics differ. A blended job average is suitable for a monthly scenario only when its price, cost and worker-hours all use the same completed-job mix. Averaging price across one mix and labor across another creates a job that never exists.

Compare three ways the monthly margin changes

Hold monthly volume at 40 jobs and fixed costs plus owner pay at $7,000.

Scenario Job price Direct cost before fee Job contribution Monthly planning profit Profit margin
Base completed-job plan $450 $180 $256.50 $3,260 18.11%
Price falls to $420 $420 $180 $227.40 $2,096 12.48%
Direct costs rise to $210 $450 $210 $226.50 $2,060 11.44%

The lower-price case loses $29.10 contribution per job after the fee adjustment, or $1,164 over 40 jobs. The direct-cost increase loses $30 per job, or $1,200 for the month. Revenue in the third row remains $18,000, so watching revenue alone would miss the profit decline.

A $480 quote with unchanged $180 direct costs would leave $285.60 contribution. At the same 40 jobs, planning profit becomes $4,424 and margin becomes 23.04%. The quote still needs customer acceptance. Include any extra work sold with it before comparing the result.

Use completed-job records to identify which change is relevant. If overruns are the cause, raising a menu price without fixing the estimate can leave the same cost uncertainty. If a service is consistently outside scope, change the written scope and approval process as well as the price.

Calculate jobs needed for the monthly goal

Suppose you also want $1,000 of target profit beyond fixed costs and owner pay. The combined goal is $4,000 + $3,000 + $1,000 = $8,000. At $256.50 contribution, required volume is $8,000 ÷ $256.50 = 31.19, rounded up to 32 completed jobs.

At the lower $420 price, the same goal requires 36 jobs. At $210 direct cost and the original price, it also requires 36. Round up because you need whole completed jobs. Planning on 31 jobs in the base case would leave the stated goal short.

If conversion from qualified inquiries to paid jobs is assumed to be 40%, 32 completed jobs require 32 ÷ 40% = 80 qualified inquiries. This is another explicit planning assumption. It does not mean every channel produces equally valuable leads or that your actual conversion will reach 40%.

Compare that goal with delivery capacity

Two workers with 35 weekly hours each and 70% utilization provide 2 × 35 × 52 ÷ 12 × 70% = 212.33 monthly delivery worker-hours. At four worker-hours per job, whole-job capacity is 53 jobs. The 32-job goal and 40-job monthly example fit this simplified hour model.

If difficult access and route travel raise duration to six worker-hours, capacity falls to 35 whole jobs. At the same time, paid labor may also rise; leaving the $180 direct-cost estimate unchanged would be inconsistent unless another cost decreases. Model both the cost and time change rather than adjusting only the capacity figure.

Weather and seasonality can affect the available schedule. Use a utilization assumption that reflects the period you are planning, and compare a shorter working month. A monthly margin measured during a strong period should not automatically become the annual forecast. Sum the expected months with their own revenue and costs when building a yearly plan.

Enter the base case in the calculator

Open the landscaping break-even calculator. Enter price $450, material cost $30, labor cost $100, other variable cost $35, acquisition cost $15 and payment fee 3%. Set fixed costs $4,000, owner pay $3,000 and target profit $1,000.

Use two workers, 35 hours per worker per week, four worker-hours per job and 70% utilization. The result should show $256.50 contribution, 32 required jobs and 53 whole-job capacity. The calculator tests the monthly goal; calculate the actual month's profit from completed jobs rather than assuming capacity equals sales.

What can make the monthly margin misleading

  • Calling contribution net profit. Monthly fixed costs and the remaining owner income still need coverage.
  • Double-counting owner wages or equipment. Explain which cost line includes each item.
  • Counting calendar hours as crew-hours. Include every worker's time and relevant travel.
  • Mixing job averages from different service mixes. Weight price, costs and duration consistently.
  • Using a profitable month as the entire annual forecast. Plan seasonality and actual availability separately.

FAQs

Which margin should I use to review completed jobs?

Use contribution after the costs that follow each job, with a consistent list of included items. Then subtract monthly fixed costs and the remaining owner-pay goal to review what the whole month leaves.

Should the owner salary be included when comparing months?

Use the same owner-pay treatment in every comparison and show it beside the result. If the owner’s field wages are already in direct labor, count only the remaining income goal in owner pay.

How do I stop counting equipment costs twice?

Write down what the job-use allowance covers and what remains in monthly overhead. Remove any overlapping fuel, insurance, maintenance or replacement allocation before calculating profit.

Why does the goal require 32 jobs rather than 31?

The $8,000 combined goal divided by $256.50 contribution is 31.19. Since completed jobs are whole units, 31 falls short and 32 meets the stated target.

What if maintenance and installation jobs have very different margins?

Keep separate job sheets first, including worker-hours. Build the monthly average from the completed or expected mix, using the same proportions for revenue, costs and time.

Can a good profit month hide a problem for the rest of the year?

Yes, the number of working days, job mix and paid volume can change across seasons. Build the annual plan from the separate monthly results instead of multiplying one strong month by twelve.

Takeaways

  • Define which costs and owner pay the margin includes.
  • Allocate equipment once, with its included items written down.
  • Use the same service mix for price, costs and worker-hours.
  • Review seasonal months separately before building the annual total.

For closer job reviews, read the landscaping job-costing guide, route density guide and crew utilization guide. More examples are in the business guides.

For a different service scope, compare Landscaping Equipment Cost per Hour: Build a Job Rate and Landscaping Maintenance Contract Pricing: Scope and Visits. Recalculate contribution and delivery time for that scope.

name: Agency
title: Agency Profit Margin: Gross, Contribution and Operating Profit
description: Calculate agency profit margin with a reconciled example. Separate gross profit, contribution, operating profit, owner pay and client delivery costs.
metaDescription: Calculate agency profit margin with a reconciled example. Separate gross profit, contribution, operating profit, owner pay and client delivery costs.
alt: Agency business owner reviewing profit margin and operating costs
imageCaption: Agency business owner reviewing profit margin and operating costs
opening: Learn how US owner-operators calculate agency profit margin, utilization, gross margin, take-home pay, and break-even revenue with real examples.
features: Gross, contribution, and net margin separated
Owner take-home kept distinct from accounting profit
Capacity and utilization checked against revenue goals
html:
Your agency profit margin improves when you price the work above its fully loaded cost and keep enough delivery capacity billable; utilization alone cannot rescue underpriced services. For most US owner-operators, the useful target is a healthy contribution margin at a sustainable utilization level, followed by enough operating profit to pay you fairly and fund the business.

The direct answer

Your agency profit margin is the percentage of revenue left after the costs required to deliver your work and run the business. The simplest formula is:

Operating margin = (revenue − operating costs) ÷ revenue × 100

Gross margin measures what remains after direct delivery costs. Those costs may include subcontractors, freelance production, paid media that you resell or manage directly, project-specific tools, and the delivery portion of employee or owner labor. If you bill $20,000 and direct delivery costs are $8,000, gross profit is $12,000 and gross margin is 60%.

Contribution margin is revenue minus variable or incremental costs. It shows how much a sale contributes toward fixed overhead and profit. A $5,000 retainer requiring $4,000 of extra labor and third-party costs contributes $1,000, or 20%, before fixed expenses.

Operating profit margin comes after the operating costs in the stated income statement. With $5,000 monthly operating overhead, that $12,000 gross profit becomes $7,000 operating profit on $20,000 revenue, or 35% operating margin. It is not an established after-tax net margin. Net profit margin uses net income after the applicable nonoperating items, interest and income taxes, divided by revenue. OpenStax distinguishes operating income from net income; classification and example checked October 17, 2026.

Owner take-home is not the same as profit. It may include salary, guaranteed payment, owner draw, or distribution. In a one-person agency, assign delivery time a target market wage even if your tax treatment differs; otherwise, unpaid job wages can look like business profit.

Utilization connects delivery hours with available capacity. If you divide by the whole paid schedule, reserve non-delivery time through the utilization assumption. If you first remove that time to create a smaller delivery-only pool, use a compatible rate for that pool. Do not remove the same hours twice.

Close the monthly margin against committed payroll

Gross margin, contribution margin and operating margin answer different questions. Direct delivery costs can include committed employee payroll. Contribution, however, depends on the costs that change under the decision you are modeling. A salary does not become avoidable because you allocate it across clients in a spreadsheet.

Consider a separate fictional agency month with four $3,000 retainers. Revenue is $12,000. Contract-specific costs are $500 per client, including the variable contractors, tools and fees chosen for this example. Total variable costs are $2,000. Committed payroll is $6,000 and other monthly overhead is $2,000.

Monthly line Amount
Retainer revenue $12,000
Client-variable costs −$2,000
Contribution before committed costs $10,000
Committed payroll −$6,000
Other fixed overhead −$2,000
Operating remainder $2,000

Operating margin is $2,000 ÷ $12,000 = 16.67%. This result is before any owner-pay goal, tax or financing costs not already included in the stated boundary. It should not be presented as an after-tax net profit figure. If owner compensation is already part of committed payroll, keep it there instead of subtracting it again.

Now lose one client while payroll and overhead remain committed. Revenue becomes $9,000 and variable costs fall to $1,500. Contribution is $7,500. Subtract the same $8,000 of committed costs and the result is a $500 loss, or −5.56% operating margin. The lost client’s short-term contribution was $2,500; allocating some salary to that client would not make the salary disappear.

This is the practical reason to keep a cancellation case separate from a full-capacity job-costing case. Both can be useful, but they need different cost behavior assumptions. Reconcile every line to invoices, payroll and an explicit period before comparing the margins.

Connect margin to monthly client capacity

To reproduce that committed-payroll model, use the agency calculator with a $3,000 client price, $500 of total client-variable expense, zero other unused cost fields, and $8,000 monthly operating overhead. In this isolated example set additional owner pay and target profit to zero. The $500 already includes any fees assigned to it, so set the percentage fee field to zero rather than charging them twice.

Contribution is $2,500 per client and operating break-even is 3.2 clients, rounded up to four. Three do not cover committed costs; four leave the $2,000 operating remainder shown above. Adding an unfunded $2,000 owner-pay goal raises financial need to $10,000, which four clients cover exactly. Adding a further $1,000 profit target requires five clients.

Now check delivery. Two people at thirty-five scheduled hours weekly and 65% productive utilization supply 197.17 productive worker-hours per average model month. At forty total worker-hours per client, capacity is 4.93 clients, or four complete commitments. Four clients fit the aggregate check; the five-client goal does not.

At the five-client financial goal, required contribution is $11,000. Four clients deliver $10,000, leaving a $1,000 gap. A plan can reach operating break-even and still fail to support the owner’s larger income goal. State which financial boundary a profitable-looking margin actually covers.

For the same four-client capacity, suppose the total variable cost remains $500 per client and fee behavior stays inside that allowance. A $3,250 price contributes $2,750 per client; four then provide $11,000. That price solves the arithmetic under those fixed assumptions, but the offer still needs buyer acceptance and the same delivery scope. If fees rise with price, separate and recalculate them instead of retaining the flat allowance.

Turn the review into one owner decision

Read margins alongside client hours rather than making utilization the target by itself. Record collected revenue for the chosen operating period, costs actually incurred, estimated versus delivered scope, and compensation already funded by payroll or labor allowances. Keep deposits and unpaid invoices visible in a separate cash view.

Then isolate the decision you are testing. If the issue is an underpriced retainer, compare a revised price or narrower scope. If the issue is committed payroll with too few clients, test qualified demand and fixed commitments. If the issue is full delivery capacity, adding leads does not create production hours. Each action should move a specific input you can verify.

Keep this review connected to agency billable utilization and agency client profitability. The client guide shows which engagement earns its share; this monthly guide checks whether the combined portfolio supports the whole agency.

How to run your own numbers

Start with a monthly view, then extend it across 12 months so annual expenses and seasonal demand do not surprise you. List revenue by client or service. For fixed-fee work, divide each fee by all expected hours to find its effective rate.

Calculate capacity by role. Begin with working hours, subtract time that cannot be sold, and divide expected billable hours by available delivery hours. Make a second calculation using total working hours to see how much of your whole job is delivery.

Separate direct delivery costs from fixed overhead, including a target cost for your delivery labor. Include contractor-related costs tied to delivery. Then calculate:

  • Gross margin: (revenue − direct delivery costs) ÷ revenue.
  • Contribution margin: (revenue − variable costs) ÷ revenue.
  • Operating margin: (revenue − direct costs − overhead) ÷ revenue.
  • Break-even revenue: fixed overhead ÷ contribution margin percentage.

For a faster check, enter your agency’s pricing, costs, and capacity into the agency break-even calculator. Reconcile its assumptions to your own spreadsheet, especially whether owner compensation is treated as a cost and whether contractor expenses are variable.

Run conservative, expected, and strong-utilization cases. Test a lost client, delayed payment, contractor rate increase, and a project taking 20% longer. A margin that works only in the strong case is not reliable.

Common mistakes

Treating owner draws inconsistently makes periods incomparable. Give delivery labor a target cost, then keep distributions separate from operating performance.

Using total clock hours as capacity exaggerates utilization. Sales and administration are necessary work, but they are not billable delivery unless a client pays for them.

Ignoring scope creep makes a profitable proposal look good on paper while the effective rate declines. Track estimated and actual hours.

Confusing gross margin with net margin hides overhead. A project can have excellent gross margin and still lose money when account management, software, insurance, and sales time are included.

Planning for 100% utilization leaves no capacity for selling, learning, recovering, or fixing errors. A utilization target should support reliable delivery and future revenue.

Agency margin should follow complete client delivery cost

Suppose fictional monthly agency revenue is $20,000 and sale-dependent delivery, contractor, fee and client-tool costs total $9,000. Contribution is $11,000, or 55%. If shared commitments and separately modeled owner pay total $8,000, the remaining plan result is $3,000, or 15% of revenue, before taxes and unmodeled expenses.

Compare client scope before comparing percentages. A contractor-heavy engagement can have a lower margin but require less internal delivery time. An internally delivered retainer may look strong while consuming many unrecorded owner hours. Record those hours and the chosen compensation boundary.

Shared software and administration should not be charged in full to every client. Use allocations for management comparison where useful, then reconcile to the actual total. A high margin does not establish enough customer demand, and a busy team does not establish healthy pricing. Review contribution, utilization and monthly commitments together.

For the next decision in this plan, compare Agency Client Concentration: Revenue, Contribution and Cash; Agency Project vs Retainer Profitability: Count the Hours; Agency Employee vs Freelancer: Find the Workload Threshold. Use each guide’s own price, cost and capacity assumptions rather than carrying one margin across different services.

Agency margins: reconcile gross, contribution and operating profit

Agency operating profit margin = operating profit ÷ net revenue × 100. Agency profitability reports often use “margin” for different subtotals. State which costs move with a client and which costs are committed. In this independent fictional month, $100,000 net revenue supports $20,000 client-variable subcontracting, $50,000 committed delivery payroll, $5,000 tools and $10,000 other operating costs. Owner delivery compensation is already included in payroll.

Three margins on the same invented agency revenue, USD
MeasureCost definitionResult
Gross profitRevenue less 20,000 subcontracting and 50,000 delivery payroll30,000 / 30%
Contribution under stated behavior scopeRevenue less only the 20,000 variable subcontracting80,000 / 80%
Operating resultContribution less 50,000 payroll, 5,000 tools and 10,000 overhead15,000 / 15%

The 80% contribution rate does not mean the agency has an 80% net profit margin. Committed delivery payroll still needs funding and is deducted once when reaching the operating result. Interest, tax, capital spending and collection timing are separate from these stated operating subtotals.

A client-level report can allocate payroll for comparison, but the client allocations must reconcile to the actual payroll total. Do not deduct the full $50,000 against every account and then deduct it again at agency level. Review profitability by client with actual delivery hours and utilization. An agency’s affordable margin follows its complete cost and capacity plan, not a universal agency-average percentage.

Compare the earnings subtotal on a consistent basis

Use the EBITDA and margin calculator only with the same reporting period and entity. Keep D&A, interest and income-tax add-backs distinct from the operating and net margins discussed here.

FAQs

What is a good agency profit margin?

There is no universal target because service mix, owner compensation, geography, and growth investment differ. Use a margin that pays a market-based owner wage, covers overhead, builds cash reserves, and leaves a deliberate profit after those costs.

Is utilization the same as profitability?

No. Utilization measures how much capacity is sold, while profitability measures what remains after costs. You can be highly utilized at an underpriced rate and earn little, or have moderate utilization with strong pricing and a better margin.

Should I include my own labor in agency costs?

Yes, for management decisions, especially when you perform client delivery. Assign your delivery time a reasonable target cost so that profit does not simply represent unpaid wages. Keep the management calculation distinct from your tax or bookkeeping presentation when needed.

What is the difference between gross margin and contribution margin?

Gross margin usually subtracts direct delivery costs, including the cost of producing the work. Contribution margin focuses on costs that change with a specific sale or client and shows how much revenue is available to cover fixed overhead and profit. Your accounting policy should define which costs go into each measure.

How do retainers affect utilization?

Retainers can stabilize revenue, but they can also hide unused or unlimited scope. Record the hours each retainer consumes, including meetings and revisions, then compare the effective hourly rate and contribution margin with your capacity plan.

What happens if my utilization is too low?

Verify your available-hour denominator and consistent time records. Then improve qualified lead flow, tighten the offer, adjust pricing, or reduce fixed costs instead of automatically adding services.

What happens to margin when a client leaves but payroll stays fixed?

Lost revenue is reduced only by costs that actually disappear. In the separate example, losing one $3,000 client avoids $500 variable cost while $8,000 committed costs remain, changing a $2,000 operating remainder into a $500 loss.

Should contractor expenses be deducted before contribution?

Include client-specific costs that change with the engagement under the chosen boundary. Committed arrangements may need a different cash treatment. Count each cost once and explain the classification.

Takeaways

  1. Price every engagement against total delivery time, not only the visible production hours.
  2. Track gross margin, contribution margin, operating margin, and owner take-home separately so one number does not hide another.
  3. Use sustainable utilization, leaving capacity for sales, administration, quality control, and recovery.
  4. Recalculate scenarios before changing your offer; a higher price, narrower scope, or better capacity mix can improve profit without simply working more hours.
  5. Treat the figures as a management model, and update the assumptions when your team, service mix, or overhead changes.

Apply the next planning step

Compare the two denominators before interpreting a pricing percentage. The widget only includes its entered cost; a price margin is not automatically agency net profit. Check margin versus markup on your defined cost basis.

answerHtml:
How to calculate an agency profit margin

Operating profit margin = (revenue − all operating costs for the period) ÷ revenue × 100. Net profit margin instead uses net income after applicable interest, taxes and other nonoperating items. Name the measure before comparing agencies or months.

In the fictional USD month below, $12,000 retainer revenue − $2,000 client-variable costs − $6,000 committed payroll − $2,000 other overhead = $2,000 operating profit, or 16.67% operating margin. This is before any additional owner-pay goal, interest or tax not already included. It is an example, not an industry average or a promised healthy margin.

Reconcile salary and per-client labor so neither is counted twice. Test client contribution, monthly commitments and agency capacity after reviewing the cost boundary below; the example is not transferred automatically.
